issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of blending does not convert property held by a Hindu female as a limited owner into joint family property.
material_facts: A woman inherited immovable property from her father and held it as a limited owner.
Members of her husband’s family dealt with the property, used some of it to provide maintenance, and obtained revenue records in family members’ names.
The evidence did not show a clear and unequivocal intention by the woman to abandon her title and make the property joint family property.
The woman later executed a deed of surrender, which was inconsistent with an intention to blend the property into her husband’s family estate.
issues.conclusion: The claim to include the inherited property in the joint family estate by blending failed because the doctrine does not apply to property held by a Hindu female as a limited owner.
issues.legal_principle: Blending requires a coparcener who owns separate property to act deliberately and unequivocally to abandon its separate character and impress it with the character of joint family property. A Hindu female holding a limited estate is not a coparcener with an interest in coparcenary property, and she cannot bypass the rules governing surrender by allowing her husband’s family to treat her limited estate as joint property. The Court held that the text of Yajnavalkya and Vijnyaneshwara’s commentary discussed in Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi (1932) concerned augmentation of common stock using that stock, not blending of independently acquired property; it relied on Rajanikanta Pal v. Jaga Mohan Pal (1923) for the recognized doctrine of blending and disapproved Shiba Prasad Singh insofar as it treated that text as the foundation of the doctrine.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is brought in a proceeding seeking division of family property.
predicates.property_held_as_limited_estate: A woman holds the property as a limited owner rather than as a coparcener.

issues.definition: When a partition proceeding concerns property held by a woman as a limited owner, that property cannot be claimed as joint family property through blending.

issues.legal_issue: Property recovered by a family manager in litigation conducted with the family’s consent and at its expense benefits the family rather than the manager alone.
material_facts: The family remained undivided, and the first respondent was its manager.
The manager joined a reversionary suit with another family member; the evidence showed that the family had been consulted and had consented to the litigation being pursued on its behalf.
The expenses of the litigation were borne from joint family funds, and the manager did not establish that he had paid them from his separate funds.
The compromise decree resulted in the manager receiving the disputed properties.
issues.conclusion: The properties received under the compromise decree were acquired by the manager as representative of the undivided family and benefited the family; the family members were entitled to share in them.
issues.legal_principle: Property obtained by a family manager through litigation undertaken with the knowledge and consent of the family and funded from joint family resources is acquired for the family, not for the manager’s personal benefit. The Court also held that when a manager in possession and control of joint family funds claims that property was acquired with separate funds, the manager bears the onus of proving that claim by clear and satisfactory evidence.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and manager_acquired_property_through_litigation and family_authorized_litigation and joint_family_funds_paid_litigation_costs

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is brought in a proceeding seeking division of family property.
predicates.manager_acquired_property_through_litiga: A family manager obtained property as a result of litigation.
predicates.family_authorized_litigation: The family knew of and consented to the litigation being pursued on its behalf.
predicates.joint_family_funds_paid_litigation_costs: The expenses of the litigation were paid from funds belonging to the family.

issues.definition: When a manager obtains property through litigation authorized by the family and paid for with family funds, the property belongs to the family.

issues.legal_issue: A manager who claims that property was acquired with separate funds must prove the separate source of those funds.
material_facts: The family manager claimed that the litigation expenses had not been paid from joint family income.
He did not provide reliable evidence that he had sufficient separate means to pay those expenses.
The evidence concerning a small earlier purchase did not establish that the litigation was funded separately.
issues.conclusion: The manager bore the burden of proving that the litigation expenses came from his separate funds, and he failed to discharge that burden.
issues.legal_principle: Where a manager in possession and control of joint family funds claims that property was acquired with separate funds, the onus rests on the manager to prove by clear and satisfactory evidence that the purchase money or relevant expenditure came from the separate fund.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is brought in a proceeding seeking division of family property.
predicates.manager_claims_separate_funding: A family manager asserts that an acquisition or expense was funded from the manager’s separate resources.
predicates.manager_controls_joint_family_funds: The manager is in possession or control of funds belonging to the family.

issues.definition: When a manager controlling family funds asserts that an acquisition or expense was separately funded, the manager must prove the separate source.

issues.legal_issue: Property validly surrendered by a limited owner to a reversioner cannot be claimed as joint family property by other family members on the basis of blending.
material_facts: The disputed properties had originally belonged to the family but had been sold in a genuine transaction and thereafter formed part of another person’s estate.
The limited owner executed a genuine and valid deed of surrender of the properties in favour of the family manager.
The validity of the surrender was not disputed, and the surrender was inconsistent with the claim that the limited owner had previously blended the properties into the husband’s family estate.
issues.conclusion: The claim to a share in those properties failed because the valid surrender was inconsistent with the asserted blending and the claimants had no share in them.
issues.legal_principle: A valid surrender by a Hindu female holding a limited estate is recognized under Hindu law. A valid surrender that is inconsistent with an asserted intention to blend the property defeats the claim that other family members are entitled to it as joint family property.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is brought in a proceeding seeking division of family property.
predicates.limited_owner_validly_surrendered_proper: A limited owner validly surrendered the property in favour of a person entitled as reversioner.

issues.definition: When a limited owner validly surrenders property to a reversioner, other family members cannot obtain a share in it by claiming it was blended into family property.
